Chapter 1: Facing the Question of Life’s Meaning
Have you ever found yourself caught off guard by a simple question—right in the middle of an ordinary day? Maybe you’re waiting for a bus, sitting at your desk, or just washing dishes, when suddenly, this odd thought floats in:
Why am I doing any of this?
Life just keeps moving along, people rush past, the world spins on, but beneath it all, there’s this quiet question that just won’t let go. It’s not really about feeling happy or sad. It’s deeper—wondering if any of it actually matters.
And you know, that’s the kind of question that can shake even the most grounded person.
Most of the time, we brush these thoughts aside. There are bills to pay, kids who need dinner, deadlines that don’t wait. But every now and then, that question lingers. It’s not just about having a rough day. It’s about the foundations of everything—why keep going, especially when so much feels random or meaningless?
This is really at the heart of what people call the “absurd”—that clash between our longing for meaning and the universe’s silence.
Sometimes, facing that feeling, people start to wonder: is life even worth living? Not in a moment of despair, but as a real, logical question. If life has no meaning, why stick around? Believe it or not, this question’s been haunting both philosophers and everyday folks for centuries.
Most of us, though, don’t dwell there for long. Daily routines, the comfort of habits, and even simple distractions help shove that big question to the background. But for some, it won’t disappear. The search for an answer becomes urgent.
Is there a way to live honestly in a world that doesn’t hand us a clear purpose?
The first step is to see the absurd for what it really is. It’s not some puzzle we can solve, but a reality we have to face. The absurd isn’t just “out there”—it’s born from the collision between our need for answers and the world’s silence. It’s that strange, unsettling feeling when things that used to make sense suddenly don’t.
Maybe you’ve had a moment—walking through the city at night, streets empty, lights flickering—and suddenly, everything feels unfamiliar. The buildings, the cars, even the sound of your own footsteps seem strangely disconnected from any bigger story. In that instant, the absurd isn’t just an idea. It’s something you truly experience.
Most people, when faced with that feeling, look for ways to escape. Some turn to religion, hoping for answers from above. Others bury themselves in work, relationships, or even pleasure. But if we’re honest, those are just ways to avoid the question—not to answer it.
The real challenge? Facing the absurd head-on, without turning away or pretending it’s not there.
And let’s be clear—it’s not easy. It takes courage to admit that life might not have an ultimate meaning, and even more to keep living anyway. But it’s only by facing the absurd directly that we can start to find a way forward.
So, here’s the question that really matters: Not whether life has meaning, but—how do we live when it doesn’t?
